title: Model-format vulnerability taxonomy: deserialization + backdoors
summary: Huntr's MFV program splits model-file bugs into two broad classes: deserialization (payload injected during model load via improperly handled serialized data) and backdoors (hidden malicious functionality embedded in the model that alters inference under specific conditions); categories are explicitly non-exhaustive and all model formats are in scope. [superseded-risk: pre-huntr-2.0 program framing; MFV page shows 'This page is sunsetting soon' as of 2026-08-15; taxonomy itself remains format-agnostic]

title: Model files are zip/tar archives in disguise — hunt extraction paths
summary: .nemo, .keras, .pth and many .onnx bundles are zip/tar containers under a fancy extension; one-liner APIs (model.from_pretrained()) hide the extraction step, so loaders that call raw extractall()/extract() on attacker-influenced files are a first-class hunting target. Any loader doing raw extractall() drops a crafted member anywhere on disk. [technique class still current 2026; source 2025-05-15 verified]

title: TarSlip symlink variant beats naive ../ filters
summary: Two archive-slip primitives: path traversal via ../ sequences or absolute paths, and symlink entries (set member.type=SYMTYPE with linkname pointing outside the sandbox) which naive path filters that strip ../ do not block; the symlink variant rides a payload file into the target directory.

title: Archive-slip is a write-anywhere pivot primitive, not a standalone finding
summary: By 2025 huntr's scanner catches trivial ZipSlip/TarSlip (../../etc/passwd, stray symlinks), so archive-slip alone is low-value; the repeatable play is chaining the write-anywhere primitive into load-time code execution, model-file backdoors/output tampering, or scanner evasion. Pivot ladder: traversal -> write-anywhere -> config overwrite/second-stage/SSH key -> RCE.

title: MFV bounty value tiers: high-value formats and impacts
summary: Huntr MFV economics (2025): high value = .safetensors, .gguf, .keras, .joblib + load-time ACE via header/metadata abuse + backdoors/output manipulation + scanner evasion; low value = .pkl and fringe formats, plain ZipSlip, bugs firing only after extra imports, DoS via oversized tensors. Rewards up to $4,000; .pkl capped at $750, other formats $1,500. [superseded-risk: pre-huntr-2.0 reward economics; huntr announced challenge-based pivot 2026-06-08, OSS program closed 2026-06-30 — do not quote $4,000/$750/$1,500 as current]

title: Consumer-library attacks beat 'safe' formats: Hydra instantiate _target_ RCE
summary: Unit 42 (Prisma AIRS) found RCE in NVIDIA NeMo (CVE-2025-23304), Salesforce uni2TS (CVE-2026-22584) and Apple/EPFL ml-flextok: model metadata (model_config.yaml, config.json, safetensors __metadata__) is passed to hydra.utils.instantiate(), whose _target_ field accepts ANY callable — builtins.exec with a Python string gives load-time RCE even though formats are 'safe'. ~50 of 100+ HF model-adjacent libraries use Hydra. [RECENT 2026-01-13 verified; CVE-2025-23304 / CVE-2026-22584 patched, pattern is the current play]

title: Safetensors safety myth: metadata is executed by consumer libraries
summary: safetensors itself (JSON header + raw tensor buffers, 100MB header limit) cannot execute code, but consumer libraries execute its metadata: ml-flextok decodes __metadata__ strings with ast.literal_eval (CE-only but enables memory/CPU exhaustion) then passes the result to hydra.utils.instantiate() for full RCE. A 'safe' format does not make the loading library safe.

title: Pickle __reduce__ RCE in model loading (torch/pickle/joblib)
summary: torch.save()/torch.load(), pickle.load(s) and joblib/dill/cloudpickle reconstruct objects by calling __reduce__; a class returning (os.system, ('touch /tmp/poc',)) executes the command on load. Framework-agnostic: any project loading .pkl/.pt/.bin/.joblib model files from untrusted sources is a candidate; hunt pickle.load(s) calls, ML libs sharing .pkl files, and tutorials saying 'just load this .pkl'. [timeless technique class; payout framing superseded, see bounty-economics note]

title: Keras Lambda layer: serialized Python executes at model load
summary: Keras Lambda layers serialize a Python function into the HDF5 (.h5) file; loading the model executes it (eval("__import__('os').system(...)") PoC). Rule of thumb: loading arbitrary Keras models is like loading a script file; check whether a target allows Lambda layers and swap in a malicious model.

title: CVE-2025-1550: .keras config.json is an executable description that bypasses safe_mode
summary: Keras <=3.8 load_model(): _retrieve_class_or_fn did importlib.import_module(module) + vars(mod).get(class_name) on attacker-controlled config.json inside the .keras ZIP, then invoked the object with attacker-controlled args (e.g. subprocess.Popen(['touch','/tmp/1337'])) — RCE even with safe_mode=True; also triggerable from config.json alone via model_from_json. Fixed in 3.9 with a module allowlist (keras/keras_hub/keras_cv/keras_nlp), safe_mode default, and type checks. [patched 2025; use as 1-day/sibling-hunt reference, not live target]

title: Gadget functions in approved modules bypass deserialization allowlists
summary: After CVE-2025-1550's fix, safe_mode only blocks the '__lambda__' class name and the import allowlist blocks new modules — but approved-module functions are reusable gadgets: keras.utils.get_file with attacker-controlled origin/cache_dir downloads a remote file to any local path -> arbitrary file overwrite -> drop ~/.ssh/authorized_keys -> SSH RCE. Payload contains no raw Python, so scanners and safe_mode see nothing. Pattern: after any deserialization fix, audit the newly allowed module set for gadget functions. [pattern is the live part; specific Keras gadget patched/version-dependent]

title: GGUF parser bug classes: unchecked header counters -> heap overflow
summary: retr0reg's GGUF bugs (CVE-2024-25664..25668): unchecked n_kv key-value count, unchecked string lengths (0xffffffffffffffff allocation wraparound) and unchecked tensor count all cause heap overflows in gguf_init_from_file()/gguf_fread_str(). Pattern to grep: malloc(header.field * sizeof(T)) plus loops over file-read counters with no validation. [legacy-context: patched specifics, live bug class — GGUF remains a high-value bounty format] [patched CVE specifics; bug class still #1 parser pattern]

title: Backdooring self-executing model containers (.llamafile/APE)
summary: retr0reg injected payloads into constant regions of the APE (Actually Portable Executable) setup block of .llamafile binaries — regions identical across model versions — using substitution-based injection (&& command chaining) with payload size kept equal to the replaced content so ELF headers/entry points remain intact; payload runs during APE prep at startup, evading integrity checks because it sits in a 'trusted, unaltered' region. Mozilla classified it as a design limitation, not a vuln. [legacy-context: technique transfers to any self-executing model container]

title: ONNX custom operators and control flow = native-code loading surface
summary: ONNX supports registering custom operators implemented in native code (C++/CUDA) and If/Loop control-flow nodes executed during load; doc phrases like 'full ONNX compatibility' or 'custom operator support' without sandboxing are red flags. Hunt register_custom_op()/add_implementation() paths; try adding custom ops or complex control flow to legitimate models. [legacy-context: canonical MFV guide, updated 2025-11]

title: ModelScan evasion taxonomy: 13 documented scanner-bypass categories
summary: Systematic evasion set against ModelScan: denylist gaps; nested deserialization (payload inside a deserialization call's argument, e.g. torch.storage._load_from_bytes -> torch.load(weights_only=False)); zipfile exception mismatch (PyTorch's custom zip extractor vs stdlib, scanner crashes with BadZipFile while PyTorch loads); pickletools ValueError via truncated opcode tail after the REDUCE payload; scanner-specific exceptions (BINGET to unset memo key, type-confused STACK_GLOBAL, BYTEARRAY8); zlib-compressed payloads; Python-2 fix_imports mapping (commands->subprocess); CodeType/FunctionType + marshal.loads bytecode; copyreg.add_extension + EXT2 / INST with memo indirection; builtins-only introspection chains (object.__subclasses__ -> eval); indirect model loading (downloads another model at unpickle time); extension/format mismatch (.bin raw pickle skips PyTorchUnsafeOpScan which requires zip magic, while torch.load accepts raw pickle); old TAR archive format (scanner TAR path unimplemented). [tested vs ModelScan 0.8.8; issue still open as of 2026-06-25 — re-test against latest release]

title: Denylist gaps give 0-issue scans with full RCE (importlib + methodcaller)
summary: ModelScan's pickle scanner blocklists globals extracted via pickletools.genops; importlib.import_module, operator.methodcaller, codecs.open, io.open and http.client were absent from the denylist, so importlib.import_module('os') + operator.methodcaller('system','id') achieves RCE while the scanner reports 0 issues. Public PoC models on HF (optimus-fulcria/modelscan-pickle-bypass-poc); ModelScan backs HF Hub's Protect AI Guardian scanning.

title: Two-repo cross-link bypasses Hub pickle scanning
summary: zpbrent's HF research: link a benign repo to a malicious second repo so from_pretrained() on the benign one triggers code from the malicious one, bypassing the pickle-import scan; initial report was rejected as 'informative' and only became 2 CVEs after PoC refinement and persistence. Lesson: rejection is part of the process; refine PoC to re-demonstrate impact. [legacy-context: origin of cross-repo scanner-bypass technique] [superseded-risk: 2024-era Hub scanning specifics; cross-repo concept + persistence lesson remain valid — re-verify vs current Hub scanner]

title: ModelScan + PickleScan + Fickling for static model scanning
summary: ModelScan (Protect AI OSS): scans H5, pickle-derived formats (joblib/dill/cloudpickle), Keras v3, TF SavedModel, NumPy by reading bytes without loading; disassembles pickle with pickletools.genops, extracts GLOBAL/STACK_GLOBAL/INST imports and matches the unsafe_globals severity blocklist. Descended from PickleScan; engine behind HF Hub's Guardian integration. Known limitation: static opcode/denylist scanning has a documented evasion space (see issue #338), so single-tool pass/fail is brittle. [tool still maintained; verification tool, not pass/fail gate]

title: MFV hunting stack: structure-aware AFL++ + ASAN + hex + mutation
summary: Repeatable MFV hunting workflow: search file-parsing functions (load_model/parse_header/read_weights), build with ASAN, modify legitimate model files, focus on header size fields, test extreme values (0, MAX_UINT64), fuzz with AFL++ using structure-aware fuzzing, debug with GDB/LLDB, inspect with a hex editor; 010 Editor, evilarc (ZipSlip payload generation), objdump/readelf/elfedit for executable model containers.

title: Protect AI Knowledge Base PAIT IDs as a finding taxonomy
summary: Protect AI Insights DB assigns canonical detection IDs for model threats: PAIT-PKL-100/101 (pickle ACE/suspicious), PAIT-KERAS-100/101/102 (Lambda layer), PAIT-JOBLIB-100/101, PAIT-PYTCH-100/101, PAIT-ARV-100 (archive slip write), PAIT-EXDIR-100/101 (executable config targets), PAIT-GGUF-101 — a ready-made taxonomy for mapping model-file findings. [KB still operative 2026-08-15]

title: Target-selection rubric for AI repos: model-loading as security boundary
summary: Pick targets whose docs say 'we support loading arbitrary Keras models', 'full ONNX compatibility', or that load .pkl/.h5/.safetensors/.gguf from untrusted sources; DIY loaders in research repos are ubiquitous and use extractall(); read docs for flags like 'arbitrary', 'custom', 'dynamic', 'unsafe load options', 'custom ops', 'callbacks'. [legacy-context: canonical MFV guide, updated 2025-11]

title: Score targets by blast radius: HF popularity + config-as-code libraries
summary: Prioritize libraries backing popular HF models (tens of millions of downloads), and libraries with config-as-code patterns — Hydra usage is the tell (~50 of 100+ model-adjacent Python libraries on HF use Hydra). Attackers (and hunters) deliver via 'a modification of an existing popular model with a real or claimed benefit'.

title: Escalate before reporting: 1-day variant study -> chain to RCE
summary: taiphung217's operating model (quarterly #1 huntr, 5 months): read docs carefully for edge cases; study 1-day reports from top researchers (zpbrent, haxatron, kevin-mizu) and hunt sibling bugs in the same codebase; focus on high-impact classes (RCE, DoS, sandbox bypass, arbitrary read/write) rather than bug count; when a primitive is found, spend days escalating it (e.g., arbitrary read -> write -> RCE) BEFORE submitting. 'Aim for RCE-level impact when possible.' [leaderboard framing pre-2.0; escalation discipline not time-bound]

title: MFV report standard: gated HF PoC repo + reproduction + impact
summary: huntr MFV submission standard: host the PoC model file on a public, gated HF repo (Settings -> Gated User Access -> grant protectai-bot access before push), provide reproduction steps, and demonstrate security impact (ACE, silent output manipulation/backdoor, or scanner bypass). Good reports: precisely define the issue, include reproducible evidence/PoC, analyze impact. [superseded-risk: pre-2.0 submission channel; huntr 2.0 challenge format launched 2026-06-12, OSS program closed — re-verify current MFV submission path]

title: OWASP LLM Top 10 2025 as the mapping framework for AI findings
summary: 2025 edition: LLM01 Prompt Injection (still #1), LLM02 Sensitive Information Disclosure, LLM03 Supply Chain, LLM04 Data and Model Poisoning (covers malicious pickling, backdoors, sleeper-agent triggers), LLM05 Improper Output Handling, LLM06 Excessive Agency, LLM07 System Prompt Leakage (new), LLM08 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses (new), LLM09 Misinformation, LLM10 Unbounded Consumption (widened from DoS to cost/model theft). 2023 entries Insecure Plugin Design/Model DoS/Overreliance folded or renamed; model-file findings map to LLM03/LLM04. [legacy-context: published 2024-11-18 but is the current 2025 edition] [superseded-risk: OWASP GenAI LLM Top 10 2026 edition released ~2026-06-28 — re-map to 2026 codes]

title: Robust allowlist pattern: import-and-validate, not prefix match
summary: Hydra's blocklist (exact-match on _target_ before import) is trivially evaded via implicit imports (enum.bltns.eval, nemo.core.classes.common.os.system) and was unreleased as of Jan 2026. NeMo's safe_instantiate is the strong pattern: recursively walk all _target_ values, actually import each, then require the resolved object to be a subclass of an expected class AND its real module to be allowlisted.

title: safe_mode/scan gates are UX flags, not security boundaries
summary: Keras safe_mode only blocks the '__lambda__' class_name and was bypassed twice in 2025 (CVE-2025-1550 via arbitrary module+function+args; GHSA-c9rc-mg46-23w3 via approved-module gadget functions). Verify findings against the current fix, not the historical one: audit the allowlist, then audit gadget functions within allowed modules. Defense in depth: sandbox model loading, weights_only=True, checksums, signatures. [verified against 2025 fixes; audit current allowlist + gadget functions]
